title: 5 ChatGPT Prompts to Supercharge Your Note-Taking (2026)
description: Five prompts that turn passive note-taking into an active learning system — using ChatGPT to process lecture notes, extract key concepts, create connection maps between topics, generate review questions, and convert messy highlights into a structured knowledge base you can actually use later.
benefit: Transform a folder of raw notes into a searchable, connected knowledge system you'll actually use.

steps.title: Process raw lecture notes
steps.promptText:
Here are my raw notes from a lecture on [TOPIC]:

[PASTE YOUR NOTES]

Process these notes into a structured format:
1. Identify the 3–5 core concepts the lecturer emphasized (not just mentioned — actually emphasized)
2. For each core concept: a 2-sentence explanation in plain English, and how it connects to the course's broader themes
3. Flag anything in my notes that seems unclear, incomplete, or potentially wrong — these are things I should clarify before the exam
4. What is the single most important idea from this lecture that I need to deeply understand?
5. Suggest 2 follow-up questions I should explore to deepen my understanding beyond what was covered
steps.whyThisTool: Processing notes within 24 hours of a lecture — before memory fades — dramatically improves retention. This prompt forces active processing rather than just re-reading.
steps.outputExpected: 3–5 core concepts with plain-English explanations, unclear/incomplete flags, the single most important idea, and 2 follow-up questions.

steps.title: Build a concept connection map
steps.promptText:
Here are the key concepts from [COURSE NAME] so far this semester:

[LIST YOUR TOPICS/CONCEPTS FROM NOTES]

Create a concept map showing how these ideas connect:
1. Identify 3–5 parent concepts that most of the other concepts are sub-categories or examples of
2. For each pair of concepts that are related, explain the relationship in one sentence ('X causes Y', 'X is a type of Y', 'X and Y are in tension because...')
3. Which concept is the most central — if I deeply understand this one, which others become easier?
4. Which concepts are currently 'orphaned' in my notes — things I learned but haven't connected to anything else?
5. Produce a text-based mind map I can paste into my notes app
steps.whyThisTool: Understanding how concepts connect (not just what they mean in isolation) is the difference between being able to answer application questions and only being able to answer recall questions.
steps.outputExpected: A concept connection map: parent categories, pairwise relationships, the central concept, orphaned concepts, and a text-format mind map.

steps.title: Generate a smart question bank
steps.promptText:
I want to create a question bank from my notes on [TOPIC]. Here are my notes:

[PASTE NOTES]

Generate 20 questions across four types:
- 5 recall questions: 'Define...' / 'List the...' / 'What is...'
- 5 comprehension questions: 'Explain why...' / 'In your own words...'
- 5 application questions: 'Given [scenario], what would...' / 'How would you use [concept] to...'
- 5 analysis questions: 'Compare X and Y...' / 'What are the implications of...' / 'Evaluate whether...'

For each question, add: (a) the correct answer, (b) the difficulty (easy / medium / hard), (c) which concept from my notes it tests. Format so I can export it to a flashcard app (front / back).
steps.whyThisTool: A question bank you build yourself from your own notes is far more exam-effective than downloading someone else's flashcards — because the act of generating questions is itself a retrieval practice exercise.
steps.outputExpected: 20 questions across 4 types, with answers, difficulty ratings, and concept tags — formatted for flashcard export (front / back).

steps.title: Summarize a reading into a usable one-pager
steps.promptText:
I need to process this reading for [CLASS]. Here's the full text (or what I've highlighted):

[PASTE TEXT OR HIGHLIGHTS]

Create a one-page summary I can use as a reference during open-book exams or as a study aid:
- Title and bibliographic info at the top
- Central argument: 2 sentences
- Key claims: 3–5 bullet points with page references where possible [format: 'Claim (p. X)']
- Key terms defined: glossary format
- One thing the author gets right and one limitation or criticism
- Connection to course: how does this reading relate to the course's central themes?

Keep the entire summary under 400 words.
steps.whyThisTool: A one-page reference beats highlighting and re-reading the original — you can review 10 readings in the time it would take to re-read 2.
steps.outputExpected: A structured one-pager under 400 words: central argument, key claims with page refs, glossary, one strength + one criticism, and course connection.

steps.title: Build a revision master document
steps.promptText:
I have notes from [N] lectures and [N] readings in [SUBJECT]. I'm going to paste them all — your job is to synthesize them into a master revision document.

[PASTE ALL NOTES]

Structure the master document as:
1. Overview: what is this course fundamentally about? (3 sentences)
2. Core concepts: a condensed definition of each major concept (1–2 sentences each)
3. Key debates: 3–5 debates or tensions in the field this course covers
4. What I need to be able to do: list the key analytical or practical skills the course expects, not just knowledge
5. High-priority revision areas: based on how much coverage the notes give each topic, flag the 3 areas with the thinnest coverage (these are likely my biggest gaps)
steps.whyThisTool: A master revision document created from your own notes is more valuable than any study guide because it reflects the specific emphasis of your course, not a generic curriculum.
steps.outputExpected: A full master revision document: course overview, concept glossary, key debates, skill requirements, and a thin-coverage flag list.

faq.q: How long should I spend on Step 1 (processing lecture notes)?
faq.a: 10–15 minutes per lecture, ideally within 24 hours. The goal is to process quickly and actively, not to create perfect notes. Speed matters more than thoroughness at this stage.

faq.q: My notes are messy and incomplete — will these prompts still work?
faq.a: Yes — the prompts are designed to work with messy, informal notes. Step 1 specifically flags incomplete or unclear sections, which turns your gaps into a to-do list rather than a liability.

faq.q: Should I worry about ChatGPT adding wrong information to my notes?
faq.a: These prompts are designed to process information you give it, not add to it. The risk is misinterpretation of your notes, not hallucination. Always sanity-check the core concepts output in Step 1 against your course materials before treating it as authoritative.
